meta.regime: The regime is unchanged in kind and stronger in degree: a physical energy supply shock priced through US real rates, with the dollar now the only currency on the board that is up against everything. Two consecutive sessions in which DXY beat all seven peers have turned a one-day observation into a weekly fact - the dollar is positive against all seven on the week, from GBP at -0.48% through to NZD at -1.63%. Crude keeps grinding higher without any haven response: WTI 103.127 is up 1.71% today, 10.85% on the week and 22.04% on the month, while gold at 4291.57 is down 1.47% on the week and silver 3.93%. The second feature is the split inside the commodity complex, and today China told us why it persists - industrial production beat at 5.2% while retail sales missed at 0.4% and fixed asset investment deepened to -7.2%. That is a supply-side China: more output, less demand, which is precisely the configuration that keeps energy bid and industrial metals offered, with copper down 6.18% on the week. Long the energy exporter against the industrial exporter remains the cleanest cross-rate axis on this board. The third feature is that the calendar compression is now upon us rather than ahead of us: the Fed decides in roughly 36 hours, the Bank of England in 53 and the Bank of Japan in 68, and all three are effectively priced - near 85% on the Fed, a 3-0-6 hold consensus on the MPC, 97% on the BoJ. When the level is bought, the only tradeable content is guidance: the dot plot, the vote split, and whether the BoJ attaches a pause.

dailyRead: Start with what is no longer in doubt. For a second consecutive session the dollar beat all seven G10 peers, and the weekly board has now caught up with the daily one: DXY is 99.640, up 0.16% today and 0.86% on the week, and it is higher against every single currency on this file over five sessions - GBP -0.48%, JPY -0.55%, EUR -0.78%, CAD -0.92%, CHF -1.11%, AUD -1.34%, NZD -1.63%. Yesterday this desk promoted USD to the top of the board on one day of price action and explicitly declined to raise it to +3 because the month was flat. That caution still holds - DXY is exactly 0.00% on the month - but the reason has narrowed to a single event, and the event is tomorrow. The day's actual news was British, and it was a miss. The August claimant count printed +27.8k against an +8.3k forecast and -11.8k previously, a 39.6k swing in one month, while average earnings including bonus decelerated to 3.9% from 4.2%, in line, employment change slowed to +67k from +83k, and the unemployment rate held at 4.9%. This is where being specific about which leg of a thesis broke matters. Yesterday's file put GBP at 0 with both tails live into a 48-hour window, the hawkish tail resting on a labour market that had refused to crack and the dovish tail on a consumer that had. The labour leg is now the one that broke: a claimant count running more than three times consensus with earnings decelerating is not a labour market that supports three MPC members voting to hike. And yet sterling fell only 0.17%, the second-best performance on the board, and it remains the best G10 currency of the week. That gap between the data and the price is the day's most informative fact, and it has a reason: UK CPI lands tomorrow at 06:00Z forecast to accelerate to 3.1% from 2.9%, and the MPC vote consensus is unchanged at 3-0-6 for a hold. The market has decided that one soft labour print does not move a committee that is worried about an energy-driven inflation impulse. So GBP holds at 0 - the hawkish tail is thinner than it was this morning, but a cut tail has not opened, and the pound is not being sold. Second, and this is a correction against this file's own stated path: JPY is cut from +2 to +1, the second cut in two days. Yesterday's entry said in terms that a Friday hike with a pause attached takes JPY to +1. The yen got there early and by a different route - it was the second-worst G10 for a second consecutive session at -0.31%, and the weekly, which had already flipped, extended to +0.55% on USD/JPY at 154.824. The monthly trade is genuinely still intact at -2.90%, and the fundamentals are the best on the board in direction: wage growth 4.7% from 4.0%, CPI 1.9% from 1.6%, core 1.8%, unemployment 2.4%, and a central bank that will lift the policy rate to a 31-year high on Friday with roughly 97% priced. But that last clause is the whole problem. A hike that is 97% priced has nothing left to buy, and two sessions of underperformance into it are not noise - they are the market telling you the position is crowded. At +1 the yen sits level with the euro, the Canadian dollar and the Australian dollar, which is what a fully-priced central bank deserves, and it converts most of the yen-cross short book from directional trades into RANGE. Only NZD/JPY survives as a SHORT with a two-point gap behind it. Third, yesterday's file set an explicit AUD tripwire - a miss on BOTH China industrial production and retail sales would cut Australia from +1 to zero through the demand channel - and today it resolved half met, which is the second time in three days that this file's own stated invalidation has come in split down the middle, exactly as Canada's CPI did on Monday. Industrial production beat at 5.2% against a 4.8% consensus and 4.5% previously; retail sales missed at 0.4% against 0.8% and 0.6% previously; fixed asset investment deepened to -7.2% year-to-date from -6.7%. Under the file's own rule AUD holds +1 and the upgrade case is not withdrawn. But the composition is worth more than the verdict. Production beating while consumption misses and investment contracts is a supply-side China, and a supply-side China is the single most reliable configuration for keeping industrial metals offered - copper is 6.3227, down 0.12% today, 6.18% on the week and 4.26% on the month, and the XCU short is now a structural expression of that mix rather than a momentum trade. The counterweight, and the reason conviction stays capped, is that the physical copper market is tight: LME available stocks fell to 107,050 tonnes on August 26 from 166,775 a week earlier, a 36% draw, against Chilean supply problems, a shut Indonesian smelter and a Congolese export ban, with AI data-centre demand still accelerating. This is a positioning and tariff-driven short against a tight physical market, which is precisely the kind of short that snaps. Fourth, the haven failure has now been running long enough to be a regime description rather than an observation. Gold is 4291.57, down 0.17% today, 1.47% on the week and 2.82% on the month; silver is 63.170, down 3.93% on the week; and they are doing this while WTI is up 22.04% on the month with the Strait of Hormuz largely closed and Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline still shut since September 11. Bullion is not being bought as insurance because the insurance premium is being paid in oil, and because the Fed is hiking into it - the entire XAU and XAG case is a real-rates case, not a risk case, and it lives or dies on tomorrow's dots. The franc is the same story told through a currency, and it is the most counter-intuitive entry on this board: Switzerland has the strongest growth and survey mix of any economy on this file - GDP up 1.5% on the quarter and 2.3% on the year, manufacturing PMI 57.1 from 53.2, services 58.3, unemployment 3.0%, CPI 0.8% - and the franc is still down 1.11% on the week and still scored at zero, because a 0% policy rate is uninvestable when the Fed is going to 4.00% and the ECB has just gone to 2.50%, and because the SNB has been explicit about its readiness to intervene against appreciation before it meets on September 24. Good economy, unownable currency. USD/CHF LONG stays the highest-conviction dollar expression on the board. That leaves the two ends. At the top, the euro holds +1 on a genuinely hawkish central bank - the ECB hiked to a 2.50% deposit rate on September 10, unanimously, with Lagarde calling it a no-brainer, lifting the 2027 inflation projection to 2.5% and upgrading 2026 growth to 0.9% - offset by an energy bill that is a direct terms-of-trade tax, with EU gas at 82.67 up roughly a third on the month and about two and a half times year-ago levels. Canada holds +1 for the mirror-image reason: it is the only G10 economy that gets paid by this shock, and it was again the best of the seven today at -0.06% with WTI up 10.85% on the week, but its domestic data is contracting outright - employment -41.7k in August, services PMI 46.8, composite 47.8, retail sales -0.8% - and the Bank of Canada is frozen at 2.25% until October 28. Energy terms of trade, not domestic strength, is the whole CAD case, which is why it beats the commodity bloc and loses to the dollar. At the bottom, New Zealand was the worst G10 for the third time in four sessions, -0.35% today and -1.63% on the week and -2.43% on the month, and it has the week's most dangerous print ahead of it: Q2 GDP tomorrow at 22:45Z, forecast at +0.1% against +0.8% previously. The RBNZ hiked on September 2 to 2.75%, its second consecutive move, but it is expected to hold on October 28 with the next step not priced until December, and the domestic picture behind that pause is stagflationary - headline inflation 4.1% driven by Middle East fuel costs, core 3.2%, unemployment rising to 5.6%, consumer confidence collapsed to 80.4 from 94.7. A central bank that has stopped hiking into 4% inflation because the economy cannot take more is the definition of a currency you are short, and NZD/USD remains the cleanest trade on this file. The shape of the book, then: three high-conviction trades - NZD/USD SHORT, USD/CHF LONG, USOIL LONG - all of which worked today; a set of medium-conviction NZD crosses that express the same bottom-of-the-board view without dollar risk; a yen book that has been downgraded to RANGE almost everywhere; and a single dominant correlated risk, which is that the dollar leg of nine separate positions resolves on one dot plot tomorrow evening.

catalysts.event: European and UK gas prices
catalysts.note: EU gas at 82.67 is up roughly a third on the month and about two and a half times year-on-year, with UK gas at 206.07 up about 35% on the month. This is a direct terms-of-trade tax on the euro area and the UK and the reason EUR is capped at +1 despite the most hawkish central bank on the board, and the third leg of the GER40 short alongside the ECB and Brent.

geopolitics: The oil channel is now doing all of the work and the haven channel is doing none of it, and after several sessions that pattern has to be read as the regime rather than as a lag. The physical position is unchanged and severe: transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains largely restricted after a series of attacks on shipping, including two supertankers struck by projectiles while attempting to exit the Strait at the start of the month, and Saudi Arabia's East-West Crude Oil Pipeline - Petroline, running roughly 1,200 kilometres from the Eastern Province to the Red Sea port of Yanbu and carrying around 5 million barrels a day that would otherwise transit the Gulf - has been shut since September 11. Military exchanges resumed at the start of this week with neither side giving ground over the waterway. The International Energy Agency has characterised the cumulative disruption as the largest in the history of the global oil market. The price response is exactly what a physical supply shock looks like and nothing like what a risk-off event looks like: WTI 103.127, up 1.71% today, 10.85% over five sessions and 22.04% over the month; Brent 107.336, up 1.57%, 9.62% and 18.12% on the same horizons; gasoline up 1.94% and heating oil 1.98% today, with heating oil now 138.51% higher year to date. Gas is the second and less-discussed transmission line, and it is the one that hits the euro directly - EU gas at 82.67 is up roughly a third on the month and about two and a half times year-on-year, with UK gas at 206.07 up around 35% on the month. Against all of that, gold is 4291.57 and DOWN 1.47% on the week and 2.82% on the month, and silver at 63.170 is down 3.93% on the week. Bullion is not being bought as insurance against a war that has closed the most important oil chokepoint on earth. There are two reasons, and both are tradeable. The first is that the insurance premium is being paid in barrels rather than in ounces, because the disruption is physical and specific rather than systemic - traders are hedging the thing that is actually constrained. The second is that the Federal Reserve is hiking into the shock, with roughly 85% priced for 4.00% tomorrow, which raises the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset at exactly the moment the geopolitical case for holding it is strongest. Real rates are beating fear, and they have been doing so for long enough that the XAU and XAG shorts are regime trades rather than momentum trades - but note precisely what that means: they are bets on the dot plot, not on the war, and a dovish Fed surprise tomorrow would reverse them even with Hormuz still shut. The FX read follows the same two channels. On the terms of trade, the shock sorts the board cleanly into currencies that are paid and currencies that pay: Canada is the only G10 economy that gets paid, which is why CAD was again the best of the seven today at -0.06% and why it beats the commodity bloc on every horizon while still losing to the dollar; the euro area and the UK are the largest net energy importers here, which is what caps EUR at +1 despite the most hawkish central bank on the board and what supplies the third leg of the GER40 short. Japan, also a major importer, has this channel largely masked at present by its own tightening cycle. On the haven side, the more important conclusion is negative: the franc is not working. Switzerland has the strongest growth and survey data on this board - GDP up 2.3% on the year, manufacturing PMI 57.1 - and CHF is still down 1.11% on the week and still scored at zero, because a 0% policy rate is uninvestable against a Fed at 4.00% and because the SNB has repeatedly signalled it will intervene against appreciation rather than allow it. Both the demand side and the supply side of the haven bid are therefore capped, which is why USD/CHF LONG is the highest-conviction dollar expression in this file. The concentrated risk is the mirror image of all of the above, and it is worth stating explicitly because it would hit many positions at once: an escalation severe enough to make this systemic rather than specific - a direct attack on a Gulf state's production facilities, or a formal closure of the Strait - would finally bid bullion rather than only barrels, and would simultaneously break USD/CHF LONG, EUR/CHF LONG, AUD/CHF LONG, CAD/CHF LONG, XAU/USD SHORT and XAG/USD SHORT. The opposite tail is just as correlated: a ceasefire or a re-opening of Petroline would take USOIL LONG, the CAD long legs and the GER40 SHORT down together. This file is long the continuation of a specific, physical, non-systemic shock.
